all_words_learned.casual_usage: Used in plain form in casual speech — 「どこいくの？」(Doko iku no?) means 'Where are you going?' You'll hear this constantly among friends.
all_words_learned.formal_usage: Becomes 「いきます」(ikimasu) in polite form. 「どこへいきますか？」(Doko e ikimasu ka?) is the formal equivalent for acquaintances or work.

similar_words.translation: to come
to return / go home
to head out / go out

all_words_learned.translation: when you're not hungry, but you eat because your mouth is lonely

all_words_learned.notes: (also said "Ku" - but avoided since it can mean suffering)
most common in everyday speech. From English. Used for phone numbers, scores, temperatures

all_words_learned.casual_usage: Dropped straight into casual questions — 「いつくるの？」(Itsu kuru no?) means 'When are you coming?' It pairs naturally with verbs like いく and くる that you already know.
all_words_learned.formal_usage: いつ itself never changes form; only the verb after it shifts — 「いつきますか？」(Itsu kimasu ka?) is the polite equivalent.

similar_words.translation: where
who
what

all_words_learned.casual_usage: いま is everywhere in casual speech — 「いまなに？」(ima nani?) means 'What are you up to right now?' and 「いまいい？」(ima ii?) is the quick way to ask 'Is now a good time?' It drops naturally in front of almost any verb.
all_words_learned.formal_usage: The word itself doesn't change in formal settings — 「いまよろしいですか？」(ima yoroshii desu ka?) is the polite way to ask 'Is now okay?' Only the verb that follows shifts into ます/です form.

similar_words.translation: already / now (signals something has changed)
right away / immediately
later

all_words_learned.what_it_is: いただきます is the expression Japanese people say — hands together, often eyes closed — before every single meal. Literally meaning 'I humbly receive,' it's directed at the food itself, the animals and plants that became it, the farmers who grew it, and the person who cooked it. There's no English equivalent because English-speaking cultures simply don't have this ritual baked into daily life.

similar_words.translation: thanks for the feast (said after eating)
thanks to your support (humble gratitude)
what a waste (the feeling of guilt over wasting something precious)

user_words.translation: when you're not hungry, but you eat because your mouth is lonely

user_words.notes: (also said "Ku" - but avoided since it can mean suffering)
most common in everyday speech. From English. Used for phone numbers, scores, temperatures

daily_words.what_it_is: 木漏れ日 names something everyone has seen but few languages bother to name outright: the dappled, shifting light that falls through a canopy of leaves. It bundles the sunlight, the leaves, and the shadows into a single word, so instead of describing a scene you just point at it with one breath. It's one of the words most often cited by Japanese speakers as 'impossible to translate' — English needs a whole clause to say what this says in three syllables.

similar_words.translation: the shade cast by a tree
a warm, sunny patch (often a cozy spot to sit)
a gentle, rustling breeze

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces on a forest walk in early summer, when you look down and notice the ground is covered in shifting circles of light instead of describing the scene piece by piece.
daily_words.bonus: Komorebi shows up constantly in Studio Ghibli-style visual language and is a favorite word among translators precisely because it can't be rendered in one English word — it's frequently listed alongside 'hygge' and 'saudade' in articles about untranslatable feelings.

daily_words.translation: buying books and letting them pile up unread
daily_words.what_it_is: 積読 fuses 積む (tsumu, to pile up) with 読 (doku, reading), with a sly pun buried inside on 置く (oku, to leave lying around). It names the very specific, slightly guilty habit of buying more books than you'll ever get through, letting them stack up on shelves and nightstands as promises to a future self. Rather than shaming the habit, Japanese gave it a name — which somehow makes it feel like a legitimate hobby instead of a character flaw.

similar_words.translation: decluttering — discarding excess to live simpler
reading (the earnest, guilt-free opposite of tsundoku)
what a waste (the guilt of leaving something precious unused)

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces the moment you eye a nightstand stack of five unread books while checking out with a sixth.
daily_words.bonus: Tsundoku dates back to satirical wordplay in the 1870s Meiji era, mocking teachers who bought books to look scholarly without ever reading them — today it's been happily reclaimed worldwide by book lovers as the perfect label for their overflowing shelves.

daily_words.translation: the fluttery, bubbling excitement of anticipation
daily_words.what_it_is: わくわく is a gitaigo — a word that mimics a feeling rather than a sound — for the bubbly, can't-sit-still excitement of looking forward to something good. The doubled syllable mirrors the sensation itself, like a little repeating pulse of anticipation building in your chest. It's one of the first mimetic words Japanese kids learn, precisely because it captures a universal feeling English has to reach for phrases like 'giddy with excitement' to describe.

similar_words.translation: the pounding-heart feeling of nervousness or excitement
restless, fidgety anticipation
a light, bouncy, cheerful mood

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces the night before a trip, a festival, or opening a package you've been waiting for, when you physically can't sit still.
daily_words.bonus: Wakuwaku is so ingrained in pop culture that it shows up in anime, game titles, and even Kirby's Japanese branding — the doubled-syllable pattern is a hallmark of gitaigo, letting a single repeated sound stand in for a whole paragraph of description.

daily_words.translation: the person or character you passionately support / your "fave"
daily_words.what_it_is: 推し comes from the verb 推す (osu), 'to push' or 'to endorse' — literally, the one you're pushing for. It's bigger than 'favorite': it names the object of devoted, semi-parasocial cheerleading — an idol, an anime character, a K-pop member, even an athlete — whose happiness and success you root for like a personal mission. The word has spawned its own vocabulary and economy, because English has no single word for 'the person I've organized part of my emotional life around supporting.'

similar_words.translation: the hobby of actively supporting your oshi (merch, events, streams)
'precious' — fan slang for something so moving or cute it hurts
the hardcore, dead-serious crowd within a fandom

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when a friend asks who your favorite idol or character is, and you end up giving a five-minute speech about why they deserve the world.
daily_words.bonus: The term exploded internationally after the hit manga/anime 'Oshi no Ko' (2023), and 推し活 has been named among Japan's buzzwords of the year — companies now sell dedicated 推し活 planners and stationery just for organizing your devotion.

daily_words.translation: the soft, plush fluffiness of fur, feathers, or stuffed animals
daily_words.what_it_is: もふもふ is a gitaigo that doesn't describe a sound at all — it conjures a texture, the kind of dense, cushiony fluffiness you want to bury your hands in. Say it out loud and the repeated 'mo' sounds practically feel soft, which is the whole magic trick of Japanese mimetic words: sound standing in for sensation. It's the word every dog-and-cat account on Japanese social media reaches for first.

similar_words.translation: light and airy softness (like a cloud or fresh pancake)
puffy, cloud-like poofiness (a fluffy sweater or clouds)
smooth and slippery (the opposite texture feeling)

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces the second someone posts a photo of their dog fresh out of a bath, or a Pomeranian mid-fluff, captioned with nothing but もふもふ.
daily_words.bonus: Mofumofu is a cornerstone of Japan's kawaii and otaku internet culture — entire pet and plush-toy accounts exist just to catalogue mofumofu things, and the word has been informally adopted by English-speaking anime fans who now just say 'so mofu' with no translation needed.

daily_words.translation: it can't be helped / there's nothing to be done about it
daily_words.what_it_is: しょうがない is the shrug you put into words — a quiet acceptance that some situation, however annoying or unfair, just isn't worth fighting. It's less resignation and more a graceful release of control, said with a small exhale rather than despair. Foreigners often flag it as a window into a whole cultural attitude: rather than raging at a delayed train or spilled coffee, you say the phrase and simply move forward.

similar_words.translation: the more formal cousin of shouganai, same 'nothing to be done' meaning
'eh, whatever, it's fine' — a lighter, lower-stakes shrug
to give up / to accept and let go of something

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces the moment your train is delayed for the third time this week and everyone on the platform just sighs, says it under their breath, and starts making other plans.
daily_words.bonus: Historians and writers often point to shouganai as a linguistic key to Japanese resilience after disasters and hardship — it's cited again and again in post-earthquake and post-war journalism as the phrase that let people accept the unthinkable and keep functioning, without ever meaning 'I don't care.'

daily_words.what_it_is: 侘び寂び fuses two related aesthetic ideas: 侘び (wabi), the quiet, humble beauty found in simplicity and imperfection, and 寂び (sabi), the mellow grace that comes with age and the passage of time. Together they describe a whole worldview — finding a cracked tea bowl, a weathered wooden fence, or a fading autumn leaf more beautiful than anything polished or new. It's less a word than a lens: nothing is permanent, nothing is finished, and nothing is perfect, and that's exactly where the beauty lives.

similar_words.translation: 'one time, one meeting' — treasuring an encounter because it will never happen again
the gentle sadness of knowing beautiful things don't last
a mysterious, profound beauty that can be felt but not fully explained

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when you notice the chip in a favorite mug or the moss creeping over an old stone step and, instead of seeing wear and tear, you see character.
daily_words.bonus: Wabi-sabi grew out of Zen Buddhism and the 16th-century tea ceremony, where tea master Sen no Rikyu prized rustic, irregular bowls over flawless imported porcelain — today the phrase has been borrowed worldwide by interior designers and self-help writers, often flattened into 'perfectly imperfect,' even though the original idea runs much deeper than decor.

daily_words.translation: "cat tongue" — being unable to handle hot food or drinks
daily_words.what_it_is: 猫舌 literally means 'cat tongue,' and it's the real, semi-serious label Japanese people use for someone who can't handle piping-hot food — the person who has to blow on their soup for a full minute while everyone else digs in. The metaphor isn't random: cats genuinely recoil from hot food, so the trait gets borrowed straight from feline behavior and stuck onto humans as a permanent personality type. It turns a small, everyday quirk — impatience with your coffee — into a cute, almost official category of person.

similar_words.translation: a hunched, slouched posture — literally 'cat back'
a crybaby — literally 'crying bug'
so busy you'd even borrow a cat's paws for help

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces the moment someone hands you fresh-out-of-the-oven takoyaki or scalding ramen and you're still nervously blowing on it while your friends have already finished eating.
daily_words.bonus: 猫舌 is used completely earnestly in daily life — people self-identify as 猫舌 the same casual way English speakers say 'I'm not a morning person,' and it shows up on dating profiles and personality quizzes as a legitimate trait, no actual cat ownership required.

daily_words.what_it_is: キラキラ is a gitaigo built from a doubled sound, and the repetition does the work: each 'kira' mimics one flash of light, so saying it twice conjures a continuous glimmer — stars, sequins, wet pavement under streetlights. It has drifted from pure description into personality territory too, describing someone whose whole vibe is dazzling, upbeat, and photogenic. Few English words let a syllable stand in for an actual visual flicker the way this one does.

similar_words.translation: shiny and brand-new (a freshly polished floor or new school supplies)
a single sudden glint or sparkle, not repeated
glossy, lustrous (skin, hair, polished wood)

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when you look up at a clear night sky full of stars, or catch a sequined dress catching the light at a party.
daily_words.bonus: Kirakira spun off 'kirakira-name' (キラキラネーム), the term for the flashy, unconventional baby names that became a hot debate in Japan, and 'kirakira joshi,' slang for young women who curate a sparkly, aspirational lifestyle online.

daily_words.translation: "good grief" — a sigh of weary, resigned exasperation
daily_words.what_it_is: やれやれ is the sound of a long exhale turned into a word — two repeated syllables carrying the tired, half-fond resignation of dealing with something predictably annoying. It's muttered under the breath, often with a small shake of the head, when something exasperating happens exactly as expected. It's less anger than acceptance: no single English phrase nails it, though 'good grief,' 'here we go again,' and 'give me a break' each capture a slice of it.

similar_words.translation: 'just as I thought' — the feeling of a suspicion confirmed
disappointment, feeling let down
'honestly' — an exasperated emphasis muttered at someone's antics

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when a friend shows up late again, exactly as everyone predicted, and instead of getting mad you just sigh, say it under your breath, and move on.
daily_words.bonus: Yare yare became internationally famous as Jotaro Kujo's catchphrase in JoJo's Bizarre Adventure — 'Yare yare daze' — turning an everyday sigh into a meme quoted by anime fans worldwide, usually rendered in English subtitles as 'good grief.'

daily_words.translation: "one time, one meeting" — treasure this encounter, it will never happen again
daily_words.what_it_is: 一期一会 comes straight out of the tea ceremony: 一期 (ichigo) means 'one lifetime,' 一会 (ichie) means 'one meeting,' and together they carry the idea that any given gathering — even with people you see all the time — can never be exactly repeated. Same people, same room, same tea, but never quite the same moment twice. It turns something as ordinary as a conversation or a shared meal into something worth being fully present for, because technically it's unrepeatable.

similar_words.translation: the invisible thread of fate or connection that binds people together
the gentle sadness of knowing beautiful things don't last
a fleeting instant, gone before you know it

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when you're saying goodbye to an old friend at the station, or sitting across from someone at dinner and suddenly noticing how good this exact moment is.
daily_words.bonus: The phrase is traced to 16th-century tea master Sen no Rikyu's circle, popularized by his disciple's writings urging host and guest to treat every tea gathering as if it could never happen quite the same way again — today it's engraved on wedding invitations and tattooed on wrists as a reminder to stop scrolling and actually be there.

daily_words.what_it_is: ぽんこつ started out as blunt slang for a beat-up, junked car — the kind that stalls at every light. Somewhere along the way it softened into an affectionate label for anyone (or anything, including robots and AI assistants) that means well but keeps fumbling: the coworker who trips over cords, the character who's brave but hopeless with directions. Calling something ぽんこつ isn't really an insult — it's almost a term of endearment for competent incompetence.

similar_words.translation: clumsy, slow on the uptake (blunter, less affectionate)
scatterbrained and klutzy, but in a charming way
a wimp or softie who folds under pressure — endearingly weak-willed

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when a friend locks their keys in the car for the third time this year, and instead of getting annoyed everyone just laughs and calls them ぽんこつ.
daily_words.bonus: The word had a second life in anime and gaming, where the 'ぽんこつキャラ' (ponkotsu character) trope — lovable but hapless robots, magical girls, and sidekicks — became a full-blown fan-favorite archetype, and VTubers now wear the label as a badge of honor.

daily_words.translation: prickly on the outside, sweet underneath — flipping from cold to affectionate
daily_words.what_it_is: ツンデレ fuses つんつん (tsuntsun, curt and standoffish) with でれでれ (deredere, mushy and lovey-dovey) into one word for a personality that swings between icy and affectionate, often toward the very same person. It started as niche anime fandom shorthand for a stock character archetype — harsh words masking a secret crush — but has long since escaped into everyday speech, describing any friend, pet, or coworker whose gruffness is obviously a cover for how much they actually care. It's beloved because it names a very real, very universal kind of affection that's too proud to just say so.

similar_words.translation: openly lovey-dovey, gooey with affection, no prickliness at all
cool and expressionless on the surface, but caring underneath — no tsun hostility
covering up embarrassment by acting tough or dismissive

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when someone snaps 'It's not like I made this for you or anything' while it's obvious they made it just for you.
daily_words.bonus: Tsundere took off through 1990s-2000s anime and dating sims and became one of the most debated 'moe' archetypes among otaku — the term has since leaked into everyday English fandom slang, where people casually call a standoffish-but-secretly-affectionate cat 'so tsundere' with zero explanation needed.

daily_words.translation: a warm, cozy, quietly contented feeling of relief
daily_words.what_it_is: ほっこり is a gitaigo for that soft exhale of comfort — the feeling of sinking into a warm bath, cradling a hot drink, or watching something small and sweet happen. It started life in Kansai dialect describing literal warmth (a freshly baked sweet potato, still steaming), then drifted nationwide into emotional territory, describing a heart that's been gently warmed rather than a body. It's the word for contentment that's mild and unhurried, nothing like the fireworks of excitement — just a quiet 'ahh.'

similar_words.translation: relaxed and unhurried, taking your time
roomy, easygoing relaxation, with space to breathe
a slow, gentle spreading warmth, physical or emotional

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces when you watch a video of a toddler and a puppy meeting for the first time, or when a stranger's small kindness leaves you smiling on the train ride home.
daily_words.bonus: Hokkori is a staple of Japanese food and travel writing — ryokan brochures and cooking shows lean on it constantly to promise not just comfort but a specific, gentle glow of well-being, distinct from the bigger words for happiness or joy.

daily_words.translation: someone who gives up on a new habit after just three days
daily_words.what_it_is: 三日坊主 literally means 'a monk for three days' — the label for someone who throws themselves into a new resolution with full enthusiasm and quietly abandons it before the week is out. It comes from the old idea that monastic life was so demanding even sincere converts would flee the temple within days, unable to keep up the discipline. Japanese people use it constantly and without much shame — it's less an insult than a shared, knowing joke about how hard it is to keep any promise to yourself alive.

similar_words.translation: doesn't last / can't keep it going
changes on a whim, fickle
grit — the stick-to-it-ness a 三日坊主 lacks

daily_words.example_context: It surfaces every January when gym memberships, diaries, and new language apps get abandoned by week two, and someone laughingly calls themselves 三日坊主 instead of making excuses.
daily_words.bonus: The phrase is old enough to appear in Edo-period writing, originally mocking men who joined a temple to dodge debt or trouble and fled the moment the shaved head and strict schedule set in — today it's printed on planners and productivity apps in Japan as a gentle, self-aware warning aimed squarely at the buyer.
